title: Mixing of the self-avoiding-walk pivot chain
formal:
Determine, up to constant factors as \(n\to\infty\), the worst-initial-state total-variation mixing time \(t_{\mathrm{pivot}}(n)\) of the following pivot chain on rooted \(n\)-step self-avoiding walks in the square lattice. The target is an asymptotic order \(h:\mathbb N_{\ge1}\to\mathbb R_{>0}\) for which there exist constants \(c,C>0\) and \(n_0\ge1\) such that
\[c\,h(n)\le t_{\mathrm{pivot}}(n)\le C\,h(n)\qquad\text{for every }n\ge n_0.\]
A step is one attempted pivot, including a rejected proposal. The exact proposal distribution and the distance threshold \(1/4\) are fixed below. This is an explicitly selected asymptotic mixing-time formulation of the source’s broader request to analyze convergence.
why: The pivot algorithm is a major sampling method for self-avoiding walks, a basic model of polymers with excluded volume. Its practical efficiency makes the absence of a matching rigorous convergence analysis especially consequential. Determining its mixing order would quantify when samples have forgotten an arbitrary initial shape, beyond the behavior of a few measured observables.

sentences: A self-avoiding walk models a polymer whose lattice vertices cannot overlap.
The pivot chain samples such walks by rotating or reflecting a tail and rejecting intersections.
This card asks for matching asymptotic bounds on its worst-state total-variation mixing time on the square lattice.
Time counts every proposed pivot, including rejected attempts, with a fixed distribution over five symmetries.
Efficient implementations and observed decorrelation do not by themselves determine this mixing-time order.

definitions:
For an integer \(n\ge1\), the finite state space \(\Omega_n\) consists of sequences \(\omega=(\omega_0,\ldots,\omega_n)\) in \(\mathbb Z^2\) such that \(\omega_0=(0,0)\), \(\|\omega_{i+1}-\omega_i\|_1=1\) for \(0\le i<n\), and \(\omega_i\ne\omega_j\) whenever \(i\ne j\). Here \(\|(x,y)\|_1=|x|+|y|\). Walks are ordered, rooted at the origin and not identified under rotation, reflection or reversal. There is no confining box or additional energy weight. Let \(\pi_n\) give equal probability \(1/|\Omega_n|\) to each walk.

In one step independently choose \(k\) uniformly from \(\{0,\ldots,n\}\) and \(S\) uniformly from these five maps:
\[(x,y)\mapsto(y,-x),\quad(x,y)\mapsto(-x,-y),\quad(x,y)\mapsto(-y,x),\quad(x,y)\mapsto(x,-y),\quad(x,y)\mapsto(-x,y).\]
These are the three nontrivial quarter-turn rotations and the two coordinate-axis reflections in Example B.5. Propose
\[\omega'_i=\begin{cases}\omega_i&i\le k,\\\omega_k+S(\omega_i-\omega_k)&i>k.\end{cases}\]
If the proposal belongs to \(\Omega_n\), accept it; otherwise keep \(\omega\). In either case the time increases by one. Fresh choices are independent at subsequent steps. In particular \(k=n\) always leaves the walk unchanged. Denote this transition matrix by \(P_n\).

The proposal maps occur with the same probabilities as their inverses, so the chain is reversible for \(\pi_n\). The irreducibility established in the source, together with the positive holding probability, gives a unique stationary law and convergence to it. Define
\[d_n(t)=\max_{\omega\in\Omega_n}\frac12\sum_{\eta\in\Omega_n}\left|P_n^t(\omega,\eta)-\pi_n(\eta)\right|,\qquad t_{\mathrm{pivot}}(n)=\min\{t\in\mathbb N_0:d_n(t)\le1/4\}.\]
The maximum includes every valid walk, not just a straight walk, an equilibrium start, or a numerically typical configuration.

The clock counts proposals rather than CPU operations or accepted pivots. Testing whether a proposed walk intersects itself is part of implementing a transition, but its computational cost is not multiplied into this mathematical mixing time. The textbook’s instruction to repeat after rejection is interpreted as proceeding to the next proposal with the old state retained, as explicitly specified in Clisby’s standard pivot dynamics. Discarding all rejected attempts from the clock would define a different chain and is not the convention here.
answer_criterion: Supply a non-circular asymptotic description \(h(n)\) and complete mathematically correct Lean-checked upper and lower bounds establishing the displayed inequalities for the specified chain. The constants must be independent of \(n\). A function defined merely by renaming the unknown mixing time is not a determination. A polynomial upper bound alone is a partial result unless it comes with a matching-order lower bound. Average cost per update, autocorrelation estimates for selected observables, empirical equilibration tests and a different sampling algorithm do not establish worst-state total-variation mixing of this chain.

context_blocks.text: Example B.5 fixes the square lattice and five allowed symmetries, proves irreducibility, and leaves convergence behavior open. The card preserves that geometry and proposal set. It makes asymptotic worst-state mixing the concrete target rather than requiring an unspecified convergence analysis.

Clisby explicitly retains the old walk on a rejected pivot and identifies detailed balance with the uniform law. The card uses that standard rejection convention to specify exactly what a Markov-chain step means.

Clisby’s work substantially improves the computational implementation of individual pivots. Its introduction and autocorrelation study distinguish heuristic and numerical performance evidence from a rigorous worst-state bound on total-variation mixing. A fast transition implementation by itself does not establish the mixing-time order requested here.

The source also mentions the Randall–Sinclair approximate sampler, which uses a different underlying Markov chain. Existence of another sampler does not determine the convergence rate of the fixed pivot chain.
